title: ‘Not Romance-bit about Nature’ Tourism, Landscape, and Industry in Britain, 1790-1810
abstract: THE REMARK ‘NOT ROMANCE-BIT’ is from Charles Lamb's letter to Thomas Manning of November 1802: ‘For my part’, he wrote, ‘with reverence to our friends northward, I must confess I am not romance-bit about Nature’. Just as important to him was ‘all the furniture of my world’: Streets, streets, streets, markets, theatres, churches, Covent Garden, Shops sparkling with pretty faces of industrious milliners, neat sempstresses, Ladies cheapening, Gentlemen behind counters lying, Authors in the street with spectacles … Lamps lit at night, Pastry cook & Silver smith shops, Beautiful Quakers of Pentonville, noise of coaches, drousy cry of mechanic watchmen at night, with Bucks reeling home drunk if you happen to wake at midnight, cries of fire and stop thief, Inns of court … old Book stalls, Jeremy Taylors, Burtons on melancholy, and Religio Medici's on every stall – These are thy Pleasures O London with-the-many-sins – O City abounding in whores – for these may thy Keswick and her Giant Brood go hang.1 But although Lamb was lyrical about London, in the hot summers of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century most Londoners were eager to escape, even if only to the wells of Islington or the nearby hills. Many families went on annual visits to the seaside, copying George III at Weymouth and the Prince of Wales at Brighton. With the Continent barred by the Napoleonic Wars, the choice of native resorts grew steadily. Sarah Spencer of Althorp, in her early twenties in 1808, wrote that the family might go to ‘some sea place, perhaps not, and if we do I think Scarborough and Weymouth are hardly far apart enough to mention them as the extremities of our indecision. Every place on the British coast has an equal chance of our presence’.2 The place she liked least, she told her midshipman brother Robert, was Brighton, ‘a Londonish town full of fine folks, barouches, princes, theatres, and public lounging rooms’. The place she liked best was Ryde, on the Isle of Wight, with its view of the ships at anchor. Here they could wander past cottages and across the great field, which on Sunday evenings ‘was full of all the fashionable of Ryde, male and female, shewing off their best dresses, and enjoying the beauty of the evening, while two sets of boys, most of them in sailors dresses, were playing at cricket’. A seaside holiday meant settling in one place, but by contrast, one particular layer of society – well-off professional men, merchants, industrialists, and gentry families – preferred to be on the move. They planned substantial ‘tours’ around Britain, often recording them in their diaries. Touring was, in part, a deliberate exercise at self-education. This essay sets out to examine a few of the things they were looking at, or looking for, and asks if they add up to a coherent vision of the nation. Was tourism linked to the propaganda of patriotism? Were tourists blinkered escapists, turning their back on the war, or on the plight of the poor? Did their tours feed new ideas of ‘Britishness’, or simply reinforce the old? Travel was not always enjoyable. Looking back on his travels, William Rose Boughton of Shropshire wrote to his father, remembering numerous journeys in stage coaches, in the course of which I travelled with a cargo of Mrs Mostyns Paraquites & Cacatoos (I do not know if I rightly spell the names of these horridly screeching Birds) and at another time with a Subject on the roof for the dissection Room at Oxford, besides having met with innumerable biped brutes and beasts.3 Braving the bipeds – though not, one hopes, the corpses – the travellers boarded their coaches. Since the 1780s a host of books on ‘Tours’ had appeared, strongly influenced by William Gilpin's ‘Observations’ of the Wye, Lake District, North Wales, and Scotland. Gilpin had written these in the 1770s, circulating them in manuscript to influential friends including Thomas Gray, William Mason, the Duchess of Portland, Mrs Delany, and Queen Charlotte (to whom the volume on the on Lakes was dedicated), before their publication in the 1780s. The exercise was crowned by his Three Essays: on Picturesque Beauty; on Picturesque Travel; and on Sketching Landscape, in 1791. Gilpin's ideal was a landscape that combined striking natural features with interesting detail, and, if possible, with historic ruins. But his tours were also a form of worship, in which nature became an emblem of God's grace. In a note to his Essay on the Picturesque, he wrote: Nature is the great book of God; in every page is instruction to those who read. Mortality must claim its due. Death in various shapes hovers around us. Thus far went the heathen moralist. He had learned no other knowledge from these perishing forms of Nature, but that men, like trees are subject to death: Ita Debemur morti nost, nostraque. Better instructed, learn thou a noble lesson. Learn that God, who with the blast of winter shrivels the tree, and with the breezes of spring restores it, offers it to thee as an emblem of thy hopes … the Power which revives the tree, will revive thee also, like it, with increasing perfection.4 Serious attention to nature as a mode of piety or spiritual search was reinforced a decade later by William Paley's hugely popular Natural Theology of 1803. The other great promoter of the movement, Uvedale Price, whose Essay on the Picturesque appeared in 1794, concentrated less on the spiritual benefits than the aesthetic, being concerned to show that the picturesque had ‘a character not less separate and distinct than either the sublime or the beautiful, nor less independent of the art of painting’.5 The study of both nature and great artists – Claude, Salvator Rosa, Poussin, Ruisdael – was essential. But Price's painterly picturesque also had a nationalistic tinge, offering a nostalgic appreciation of elements of the British landscape lost in the vogue for improvement. He notes that painters are fond of making studies ‘from old neglected bye roads and hollow ways; and, perhaps, there are few spots that, in so small a compass, have a greater variety of that sort of beauty called Picturesque’.6 These odd, forgotten corners are valued for their intricacy, light and shade, winding ways and sudden turns, broken banks and irregular verges: this is a man-made landscape, with the untidiness of a much-worked countryside – the ‘real’ as opposed to a Reynoldian or classical ideal. Artists took note. Turner, for example, began his career making sketches based on the standard picturesque tours. His prints appeared in magazines, such as the Copper Plate Magazine (which paid 2 guineas a drawing), and he continued in this profitable vein up to his Picturesque Views in England and Wales (1825-38). In 1794 he captured the admired blend of nature and heritage perfectly in his sketch of Tintern Abbey, whose crumbing, foliage-covered walls embodied Gilpin's sense of it as ‘a very inchanting piece of ruin. Nature has now made it her own. Time has worn off all traces of the rule: it has blunted the sharp edges of the chisel; and broken the regularity of opposing parts’.7 It was on a return visit to Tintern, of course, that Wordsworth mused more intently on nature and history in his ‘Lines Composed a few miles above Tintern Abbey’ in 1798. His greater maturity since his first visit five years before, he believed, had taught him ‘ to look on nature, not as in the hour / of thoughtless youth; but hearing oftentimes / the still, sad music of humanity’. Turning away, perhaps, from the pressure of war and the crushing of radicalism, he finds here a release, an intense, physical sense of an all-enveloping presence, a sense sublime Of something far more deeply interfused Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, And the round ocean and the living air, And the blue sky, and in the mind of man; A motion and a spirit, that impels All thinking things, all objects of all thought, And rolls through all things.8 For most people, however, Tintern remained simply a ‘tourist attraction’, to be viewed according to the guide book. In 1808, after she married the banker Meyrick Hoare, Sophia Thrale (daughter of Hester Thrale Piozzi) described how they went by boat to the Abbey, ‘where the Carriage and Saddle horses met us with our cold Dinner, which after having contemplated the beautiful symmetry of this very fine old ruin’, they settled down to dining ‘most agreeably in the Grotto opposite the View’.9 This kind of comfortable tourism was increasingly popular with the upper ‘middling classes’. But the tours themselves were subtly changing. From the early 1790s on, the travellers wanted to see two different kinds of things: not only picturesque scenery and heritage – mountains and lakes, ruins, abbeys, and country mansions – but also the wonders of the modern, industrial, commercial world. James Oakes, a yarn merchant and banker of Bury St Edmunds, was a typical self-improving tourist. From 1800 he often left his business in the charge of his son Orbell and travelled round the country for weeks at a time – to Liverpool and the Midlands, to Kent and Sussex and the Isle of Wight (‘travelld 545 miles on horseback’, he wrote proudly in 1806).10 Oakes enjoyed country mansions, statues and paintings, gardens and hothouses, and the ‘enchanting and romantick’ scenery of the Peak District. The Derbyshire itinerary, stuffed with cliffs and gorges and stalactite-filled caves, like Peak Cavern near Castleton, had been popular since the late seventeenth century, and had been given a ‘sublime’ air by the paintings of Joseph Wright in the 1780s. title: Anti-Racism and Kant Scholarship: A Critical Notice of Kant, Race, and Racism: Views from Somewhere , by Huaping Lu-Adler
abstract: Immanuel Kant viewed himself as the first person to have properly defined the concept of a human ‘race’. He distinguished four human ‘races’ and ranked them: placing ‘whites’ at the top, he arranged the others in terms of alleged deficits in their capacity for thought and action. He made equally abhorrent claims about race-based slavery and white colonial rule, accepting both. Over the past few decades, Kant’s position on these matters has been the subject of increasing debate, including the question whether he retracted this racial hierarchy later in life, as I have argued (Kleingeld 2007, 2012, 2014). Huaping Lu-Adler’s Kant, Race, and Racism: Views from Somewhere is the first Anglophone book-length discussion of Kant’s views on race and related issues. In this book, she ‘interrogates Kant’s philosophy with a deep focus on his theory of race and his relation to racism’, also addressing the question of ‘what one can do to confront racism today and what, if any, resources Kant’s philosophy can still offer to this end’ (p. 1). In the following, I first provide an overview of her argument, identifying several issues that I will subsequently pursue in more detail. The book has three parts. In Part I, ‘Reframing the Discourse’, Lu-Adler criticizes critical race theorists, Kant scholars, and Kantians alike for focusing on the question whether there is a contradiction between Kant’s core moral theory and his racism (Chapter 1) and for focusing on Kant’s texts in abstraction from his impact on the formation of racist ideology (Chapter 2). Part of her aim is to ‘free’ scholarship from the ‘steadfast hold’ of the thesis that Kant changed his position on race-related issues in the mid-1790s (p. 36). In Chapter 1, she argues that Kant’s racist views are harmoniously integrated in his overall system. His moral theory, she argues, considers human beings merely qua rational beings, and the moral principles of the Groundwork ‘are not concerned with concretely embodied humans at all’ (p. 14). Kant’s racial views, by contrast, concern human beings qua embodied, and they have their proper systematic place in his physical geography. Since they deal with different subjects, Kant’s moral theory and his racial views are ‘perfectly consistent’ (p. 34). I will challenge this argument below. In Chapter 2, Lu-Adler argues that the debate over Kant’s racism has focused too narrowly on Kant’s philosophical views and has overlooked his impact on the formation of racial and racist ideology. She criticizes authors who discuss Kant’s racism for employing inadequate definitions of racism. She finds Sally Haslanger’s conception of racism as a matter of a racist-ideological formation, understood in terms of social practices, most helpful. With regard to Kant and racism, Lu-Adler suggests, ‘what matters most’ is that Kant was powerfully positioned as a scholar and educator and ‘injected’ his racial views into the social world, such that they could receive active uptake (pp. 105-106). While reading the first hundred pages, I was expecting that Lu-Adler would eventually offer a historical account of Kant’s influence on racism. But she explains that she is ‘not asking that we determine Kant’s actual causal impact in the racist-ideological formation’ (p. 105, emphasis in original), since this is impossible to reconstruct. She restricts herself to the claim that Kant contributed to racist ideology, or that we can ‘at least expect’ he did and ‘imagine’ how it went (pp. 105, 102, emphasis added). Lu-Adler concludes that ‘we’—I assume she means to include Kant scholars and Kantians—‘should not dwell’ on issues such as whether Kant’s racism contradicts his core moral theory or whether he radically changed his views. These issues are ‘beside the point’ (p. 40) and ‘can blind us’ to what really matters, which is that Kant contributed to racism (p. 88). She claims that we should go beyond, if not disregard, the question of whether Kant later retracted his own racist views. For, even if he did, he could never single-handedly undo the racialist and racist worldview that his geography and anthropology teachings and writings might have helped to form in the minds of his broadest audiences. (p. 75) I return below to this claim and to the issue of Kant’s impact. Part II, ‘Seeing “Race”’, examines Kant’s theory of race in its historical context. Chapter 3 offers an informative account of how Kant approached race as a natural scientist and how this approach fits with his theory of scientific inquiry. The biological concept of race was supposed to help solve puzzles about the heredity of bodily features that are not part of the essence of a species. More specifically: if all humans descend from common ancestors, how did their offspring develop different heritable colours? Kant hypothesized that the human species originally had a set of general ‘germs and predispositions’ that developed differently, hereditably, and irreversibly in different climates. Examining his account of the role of hypotheses, Lu-Adler argues that his theory of race is an integral part of his theoretical philosophy. Living in Königsberg, Kant relied on testimony for information about human beings elsewhere on the globe. Chapter 4 describes the emergence of standardized global data collection. Starting in the seventeenth century, European agents and merchants were given long lists of questions to answer during their voyages. With an engaging discussion of Bacon, Boyle, Linnaeus, Buffon, and others, Lu-Adler shows that these responses were systematized in terms of an increasingly narrow set of criteria, eventually leading to racialization based primarily on skin colour. At this point Kant enters her narrative, defining ‘race’ as a biological category and embedding racial differentiation in an overarching historical narrative of human progress achieved by ‘whites’ (or, as I should like to qualify, white males). These discussions in Part II are informative and interesting. Readers not already familiar with Kant’s writings on race might have liked to hear a bit more about the substance and development of Kant’s account of the four ‘races’, the status of so-called ‘mixed races’, and the geography of race (such as the fact that Kant does not equate ‘whites’ with ‘Europeans’ but includes Africans north of the Sahara, Arabs, Turks, Persians, and ‘all other peoples of Asia who are not explicitly excluded’, VvRM 2:432; cp. BBMR 8:93). But of course, there is always more that can be said. More controversial, however, is Lu-Adler’s description of Kant’s views of the mid to late 1790s. She contends that Kant never shows clear concern about the treatment of the enslaved individuals in the European colonies (pp. 235-236) and that he displays ‘cold indifference to the atrocities suffered by human beings in concreto’ throughout (p. 28). If he expresses misgivings about race-based slavery and colonialism in the mid to late 1790s, she claims, his main concern is that these have negative consequences for Europe (pp. 231-236). I return to this thesis below. Part III, ‘A Worldview Transformed by “Race”’, addresses how the modern invention of race pervasively transformed both social relations and individual self-perceptions. Chapter 5 analyses two remarkable German novellas from the first two decades after Kant’s death, both set in revolutionary Haiti. They are striking for their extraordinary perceptiveness regarding the different ways in which racialization impacts those who are differently situated in a racialized world. One novella includes apt portrayals of double consciousness avant la lettre. Lu-Adler uses this well-chosen background to warn against ‘colourblind’ accounts that abstract from race in a world that is thoroughly shaped by race concepts. Chapter 6 addresses the formation of ‘the’ philosophical canon, in particular the idea that ‘real philosophy’ started with the Greeks. Building on Peter Park (2013) and work by others, Lu-Adler draws attention to eighteenth-century German pluralist histories of philosophy that included Chinese, Indian, and Persian traditions. title: Mismonumentality
abstract: Hurrying in from the side entrance in the late months of 2019 to early 2020, a visitor to London’s Tate Modern art museum might well have missed the clamshell washed up into the Turbine Hall, especially if they were eager to get to the monumental fountain commanding the main space.1 Instead of conveying the goddess Venus, as one might expect, the shell appears to be empty. Look closer at the spot where a pearl might be luminously cosseted, and there is a hole just big enough for a small, upturned face to peer back. Look closer still and a tear trickles a slightly darker way down the white plaster of this youth’s face. To see it, you have to get so close that you might reach out and wipe the tear away. Does this person have a name or a place to call home? Is this clamshell a shelter, or a trap that has squeezed shut? To whom does this “face at the bottom of the well” belong?2 Kara Walker, Fons Americanus, 2019, sculpture installation, Hyundai Commission, Turbine Hall, Tate Modern, UK. © Kara Walker, courtesy of Sikkema Jenkins & Co. and Sprüth Magers. Photo by Tate. Nontoxic acrylic and cement composite, recyclable cork, wood, and metal. Grotto: 10.8 x 10.2 x 10.5’ (3.3 x 3.1 x 3.2 m). “Shell Grotto,” as the clamshell is named in the supplementary material to Kara Walker’s Fons Americanus, speaks to the history of one location in the extensive and extractive geographical scope of the British Empire. Bunce Island was once a British commercial fortification in the Sierra Leone River and one of the most lucrative trading posts of enslaved people in West Africa.3 The ruins of the fortifications have since become entangled with the contemporary tourism economy of Sierra Leone. Walker recounts a tour guide’s banal commentary of the ruins, including a well into which rebellious slaves were thrown: “Hole of the Brave,” the narrator monotonously intones over the redundant strains of a New Age spa soundscape, where “Captured natives, who refused boarding, were tortured and dropped to extermination.” He segues nonchalantly to remind the viewer that “Today Banana Island is peaceful, with five low-key ‘chillout’ beaches and restaurant[s].”4 “Looking,” as Christina Sharpe reminds us with respect to the history and archives of transatlantic slavery, “makes ethical demands on the viewer; demands to imagine otherwise; to reckon with the fact that the archive, too, is invention.”6 Looking is therefore consequential in the making of public memory and in bearing witness to parts of the past that have been sunk to the ocean bed or are so embedded in the walls of institutions as to be invisible. Given such commitments to collective amnesia, the visual landscape and the kinds of looking available to the public are still steeped in the imagination of imperialism. In the United Kingdom, efforts toward official or institutional public remembering of those who were enslaved—whose lives, labor, and land were stolen and exploited—have been limited.7 Making public memory of empire is a contested and active process, for which monuments serve as an excellent site since they intervene in public space at scale. Thus, Kara Walker’s Fons Americanus appeared in a moment in which multiracial coalitions of people in enslaving nations were taking histories of empire, told through monuments, into their own hands.8 Walker describes her prestigious Turbine Hall commission as “a one-person version of a nineteenth-century World’s Exposition.” The World’s Fair, she goes on to explain, “was a [form of] public entertainment exploiting the wealth and bounty of rich nations, often literally carried on the backs of its colonized subjects.”9 Walker plays with the contradiction of an individual artist’s attempt to mount and display the world but gestures to the further complexity of a Black woman artist upending the historical position into which this form of entertainment would have inserted her—that is, as an object of speculation, fetish, derision, and disgust. Historian Sadiah Qureshi observes that, while the display of living peoples has been documented since the fifteenth century in England, the growth and material expansion of empire in the nineteenth century had an enormous influence on the nature of the spectacle.10 The popularity and commercial success of such human displays culminated in the Great Exhibition at the Crystal Palace, in Hyde Park, in 1851. Invoking the exhibition culture of the nineteenth century, Walker invites us to interrogate how these histories of displaying colonized bodies as spectacle, as well as how regimes of colonial looking, persist into the present. As with her (in)famous work with silhouette, Walker’s commentary on remembering empire with Fons Americanus thrusts her viewer into murky affective territory.11 She inquires about relationships to and positions within long histories of a kind of metropolitan viewing of humans as colonial spectacles. Of Fons Americanus as complex lieu de memoire, Walker recounts: “I have created a space for reflection, joy even, amid the miasma of conflicts, racial, economic, cultural, that lodge themselves in our collective gullet.”12 Yet Fons Americanus holds out another set of possibilities for imagining the history of transatlantic slavery via the idea of mismonumentality—that is, how the artwork drafts and engages “a space of … joy even amid the miasma” for those who live in the wake of this history. As we shall see, Walker’s making of space to reflect and to experience joy consists in posing questions about representation: what parts of history can and cannot be depicted, and how to acknowledge the parts of history that cannot be represented.13 Alongside the stand-alone clamshell sculpture “Shell Grotto” and wall text posing as an advertisement for Walker’s send-up of the World’s Fair, the third and central feature of Fons Americanus is the eponymous fountain. It has two concentric pools from which emerges a pedestal, crowned by a figure of a woman. Across the fountain, Walker has assembled a “motley crew” of characters, the flotsam and jetsam of colonial modernity.14 Potential stories and fragments of stories about these figures, as individual vignettes or in relation to one another, proliferate. Single or grouped figures are depicted as drowning, half-submerged, a bit submerged, weeping, standing, seated, fleeing, squatting, laughing, kneeling, scuba diving, rowing, mourning. Walker invites us to read these figures without a commitment to verisimilitude.15 Too, the fountain’s panoply of figuration is loaded with the history of representing Black bodies in the Western art-historical tradition. British historian Madge Dresser observes that the history of empire is unevenly remembered in the physical space of London. She argues that “a significant proportion of the individuals commemorated by public statues in London during the long eighteenth century had important links with the slave trade or plantation slavery.”16 Dresser argues how little the suffering of enslaved people and the extraction of their labor are represented, even in the public memorials to abolitionists.17 The challenge of Fons Amercianus, then, is not merely to a single sculpture group, as in Thomas Brock’s 1911 monument to Queen Victoria, which inspired Walker (though it is possible to track her correspondences, send-ups, and parodies of this specific monument, especially in its representation of Victoria, which is discussed below).18 More importantly, Fons Americanus urgently queries what the absence of acknowledging the history of transatlantic slavery in London’s visual world does to public remembering about empire. This lacuna in representation is not a natural forgetting—that is, an incidental fact or ideologically “neutral” phenomenon.19 Into a carefully curated visual context of forgetting, Fons Americanus keeps the spectacle of power in full view, bringing our attention to what is suppressed in the displaying, constructing, and narrating of history as material conquest of empire.20 Furthermore, considering the work of Fons Americanus in aesthetic terms is a way to track the concept of mismonumentality as a critique of the historiography of empire. I suggest that it formulates a determinate negation of monumental historiography in the Adornian sense, as philosopher and sociologist Gillian Rose has it. She writes that determinate negation is “a criticism of society which is positive (determinate) in that it aims to attain and present knowledge … insofar as that is possible, but not positive in the sense that it confirms or sanctions what it criticizes.”21 As such, we can understand precisely how Fons Americanus constitutes a monument to the history of the Black Atlantic. Fons Americanus wagers that it is possible to gain traction on and work against monumental historiography of empire, immanently. In this, Walker shares American historian Saidiya V. Hartman’s insistence that the monumental as historiographical form can be turned against itself and its commemorative goals as “official” memory making.22 Like Walker, Hartman is curious about the negative space of historiography—the discursive voids that are essential to the ideological structuring and writing of history. Fons Americanus is motivated by Hartman’s desire to render eloquent the “cultivated silence, exclusions, relations of violence and domination” that are encoded in monumental historiography when it is presented as dominant memory making. The accompanying wall text participates in Fons Americanus’s “performance of monumentality,” to borrow a useful analytical term coined by art historian Mechtild Widrich.23 The wall text purports to be an advertisement for a nineteenth-century or early twentieth-century public spectacle such as a world’s exposition or world’s fair through archaizing diction (such as Walker’s use of first-person plural pronouns) and typography. If at first glance the wall text directs a viewer to interpret the fountain with admiration (“to marvel and contemplate”), then the second and third line rewires that affective cue. Come, One and All, to Marvel and Contemplate The Monumental Misrememberings Of Colonial Exploits Yon The second line explicitly advertises a relationship between Fons Americanus and monumentality around the formation of collective memory. Moreover, in advertising the fountain as a site for “misremembering,” the wall text describes the extent to which the fountain’s fictive efforts depart from historical veracity—they are monumental departures from an attempt to capture history or to preserve or to remember in legitimatizing ways. “Misremembering” denaturalizes the givenness of collective memory, especially about the history of the transatlantic slave trade. In pointing to the fabricated quality of remembering, Walker finds an opening for the imaginative lease of Fons Americanus to creatively misremember the history of transatlantic slavery via the forms in and through which the British Empire has been held up as glorious spectacle. Consequently, I call Fons Americanus’s immanent critique of the dominant historiography of empire a “mismonument.” The prefix “mis-” pinpoints Walker’s subversion, simultaneously indicating a knowing about the protocols of representation as well as the intention to disarrange and to rewire.24 By articulating mismonumentality in this way, I am not implying that monuments can only organize hegemonic narratives. Monuments perform a vast range of meaning-making work, and as such many large-scale artworks to empire do indeed hold subversive capacities and commentaries on empire. Specifically, however, Walker’s parodic gambit—Fons Americanus’s re-presentation of the Victoria Monument—concentrates the potential to critique empire in restaging its celebratory forms, risking even reinstating some of the power of imperial representation. In coining “mismonument” as a decisive intervention in the public remembering of empire, I recognize that many artworks might fall under this rubric, of which Fons Americanus is but one example. Unlike many other monuments whose formal politics are tied up with material claims on and of permanence, Fons Americanus was planned with obsolescence in mind.25 Its provisionality allows for experimentation with tone and subject matter, for wrecking the formal permissions and protocols of normative representations of empire. Such temporariness thus reenacts the drama of remembering the transatlantic slave trade: it reveals the mechanisms of ongoing cultural forgetting and repression that occasionally make contact with “real” historical events but more commonly traffic in desires to see Black bodies as spectacle, as commodity, as fetish. Now that Fons Americanus has been taken down from the Turbine Hall, reassembled elsewhere temporarily or broken down for parts, I am curious about how temporariness is part of and exacerbates its work as “mismonument.” Finally, mismonumentality refuses colonial demand for clear representation. title: “Unnerving to Hear this Ice Break”: Landscape and Change in Peter Maxwell Davies’s Antarctic Symphony
venue: ISLE Interdisciplinary Studies in Literature and Environment
abstract: During his trip to the Antarctic in the 1997/8 summer season, English composer Peter Maxwell Davies (1934–2016) was struck by the sights and sounds of the icy landscape. As he crossed the Drake Passage on the RRS James Clark Ross, he spoke about the intensity of the experience of being in the pack ice as the ship approached the islands. He particularly emphasized “the emptiness, the whiteness, the purity of the air, the sound of silence, the physical impact of the ship crashing the ice as it goes through the soles of your feet, right into your brain” (Davies, DF 61.B4, 04:11:32–04:14:10). This statement is just one example that demonstrates the effect that Davies’s time in the Antarctic had on him; his trip ultimately led to a published version of his Antarctic diary and five compositions, most notably the Antarctic Symphony (2000).1 These musical depictions of the Antarctic were affected by the external agendas that shaped his time in the region, as were his written and documentary comments about his experiences. Scholarship about Davies’s Antarctic visit and his resulting musical output is limited. Though the trip and symphony were commissioned by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as a way of increasing public investment in their activities, the circumstances that led to the project have not been fully considered, nor has the visit’s impact on Davies. Drawing on ecocriticism, environmental history, and environmental studies, I use Davies’s Antarctic Symphony as a case study to argue that sonic depictions of landscapes have been and still are colored by imperial and neo-imperial agendas such as those explicated by environmental historian Adrian Howkins in Frozen Empires (2017). The changes that Davies observed in the Antarctic played an important role in his own considerations of the region, its history, and its future, and these all appeared in his writings (musical and otherwise). Davies’s trip was spent on islands that are significant to British Antarctic history. Additionally, because the region is historically uninhabited, the effects of elements that shape it (such as exploration, international governance, and climate change) are more evident than in places with a longer record of human influence. The relatively abbreviated history of human impact in the Antarctic enables considerations of its real and imagined landscapes and sonic engagements with environmental disruption to be mapped onto other parts of the globe, as similar approaches can be seen in the treatment of other places that are often part of the same imperial network.2 Davies’s symphony provides a useful Antarctic case study because of how he incorporated the region’s history and ecology into the work. The Antarctic region has been a source of fascination for the British since the eighteenth century. Because of its promise of wealth in the form of whaling and sealing and the uncertainty surrounding then-hypothetical land, explorers sought resources and territory that had not yet been claimed by other European colonial powers. Both before and after the continent’s official discovery in 1820, the polar and sub-polar south attracted explorers who saw their expeditions to the region and its islands as a means of securing their own reputations or, in the case of whalers, their fortunes.3 The Antarctic has since continued to be important for commercial and geopolitical exploits, and it has proven to be culturally compelling in art, literature, and music.4 The people (primarily men) who have explored the larger region have been venerated for their scientific discoveries, supposed heroic exploits, and embodiment of British cultural values.5 British activity in the region in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries encouraged expeditions that furthered agendas related to whaling and territorial expansion (like those of James Cook and James Clark Ross). As Antarctic historian Ben Maddison demonstrates, this focus was because interest in the southern region was driven more by motives of acquisition rather than inquisition, meaning that scientific pursuits were much less of a priority than those that furthered colonialist and capitalistic expansion. British expeditions had a distinct advantage over those from nations like Russia, France, and the United States in these endeavors because of its naval power and the territories and peoples that it had already claimed in the Southern Hemisphere. These contributed to British imperial networks, which Maddison describes as “circuits of necessity” due to the logistics required for excursions into polar waters; they enabled ships to use colonial outposts on islands throughout the Southern Hemisphere to restock provisions, carried out repairs and maintenance on ships and equipment, and replaced crew members, often through demonstrations of power (10; 22–54). “Circuits of necessity” enabled longer expeditions with fewer upfront costs as the British Empire expanded. This kind of colonial exploitation in pursuit of Antarctic territory increased into the twentieth century and continues in a neo-imperial sense today, as is evident in multi-disciplinary scholarship.6 Though much of the focus on Antarctic imperialism engages with early expeditions or the so-called “Heroic Age” of exploration (1895–1917), the institutions that were established in the mid-twentieth century for the administration of British interests in the South Atlantic derive from similar motivations as those of many earlier expeditions.7 For example, during the Second World War, interest in the South Atlantic increased significantly in part due to Germany’s attacks on Allied ships in the region. Additionally, Germany, Argentina, Chile, and the United States all conducted operations and made claims to parts of the Antarctic just prior to or during the war, and Britain responded in kind with Operation Tabarin. Tabarin established multiple bases in the Antarctic Peninsula (including, notably, Port Lockroy on Goudier Island) where men overwintered and carried out research and mapping surveys in the surrounding area. The operation became the Falkland Islands Dependencies Survey (FIDS) in 1945, which in turn became BAS in 1962.8 These iterations of the agency were overseen by the Colonial Office until 1967, at which point BAS was transferred to the Natural Environment Research Council. BAS remains invested in its own history, scientific work, and legacy. This commitment has driven many of its endeavors, including the decision to commission Davies, who is well-known in British art music for his symphonic output and environmental compositions (British Antarctic Survey, “Programme Notes for the Antarctic Symphony”; McLain, “A New Antarctic Symphony”). In 1995, amidst restoration work at Port Lockroy, BAS began the process of commissioning the symphony. BAS was looking for a high publicity project that would draw attention to British scientific endeavors in the region and that would interest the public in Antarctic history and ecology. The decision to approach Davies for the symphony commission was primarily rooted in his reputation for composing environmentalist and place-centric works and his high visibility in the British arts scene. Davies’s known interest in English composer Ralph Vaughan Williams (1872–1958) also contributed to the preference, as BAS was interested in commemorating Vaughan Williams’s music for Ealing Studios’ Scott of the Antarctic (1948) and his Sinfonia Antartica (1953), both of which they knew Davies to have seen and heard and found profoundly impactful (McLain, “A New Antarctic Symphony”; McLain, Letter to Freedman; BBC Radio Scotland, 1998).9 Davies and his manager, Judy Arnold, spent nearly a month in the Antarctic under the aegis of BAS as part of the commission. BAS captured documentary footage throughout the trip and arranged specific site excursions and interviews. Davies’s time on specific islands in the Antarctic Peninsula (see Fig. 1) gave him an increased understanding of the region’s history and ecology in ways that are evident in musical and non-musical output from his visit. title: Actions toward Modern Japanese National Consciousness: The Case of Ryūkyū-Okinawa
abstract: […]Previous scholarship has shown that an explanation of the formation of modern Japanese national consciousness is, on the whole, no easy task. This is because a theoretical and empirical explanation of that political process can come only after clarifying the different levels in the structure of the modern Japanese state’s consciousness. In this article, “modern Japanese national consciousness” refers to the ideology of and policies toward the unification of national subjects that the state and government designed to produce that national consciousness. It also refers to the philosophical leanings that were created as a result within citizens’ minds.Properly speaking, there is almost never common ground between the intentions of government policy and the consciousness of citizens. From the perspective of maintaining the relations of domination and subordination essential to governing, it is more natural to find opposition and antagonism. In the actual political process by which policy takes shape in society, diverse configurations of factors fuse, separate, and change unceasingly. Rather than treat center-periphery relations as concepts of geopolitics or geography, this article sees both of those poles as weighed down by a dissonance and difference in consciousness. In other words, I not only focus on how the central government’s ideas for policy infiltrated into the regions, but also examine the roles played by a region’s uniqueness and the mutual relationship of center and periphery in that process. In one sense, this approach is an attempt to recognize the true condition of local politics as they exist within mutual relations of domination and subordination.Until now, the placenames of Ryūkyū and Okinawa have been used separately. Their parallel and simultaneous use is extremely rare, but I would like to use them consistently in this way as an academic phrase and as a geographical and historical concept. When the Okinawa region (Ryūkyū-Okinawa) is the object of investigation, conceptual phrases like “parity with the mainland” and “parity with other prefectures” reflect the imagination that the government’s laws and policies were already completed, existing while incomplete, or in a state of ongoing progress in other prefectures. For a modern state, the implementation of uniform law in regional areas that ignores local conditions will be rejected; even if compelled through military and physical coercion, more control in the long term will be achieved only with increasing difficulty. Further, the ruling classes’ sense of beneficent superiority toward the subjugated classes is already implied in those discourses about regions that have no choice but to participate in national life belatedly.The implementation and application of nationally uniform legislation to the Okinawa region (Ryūkyū-Okinawa) should be emphasized in discussions of the formation of both the state’s intentions and Japanese national consciousness. This is because the emergence of the modern nation-state means the establishment of a centralized government predicated upon the domination of nationally uniform and unified laws. Any government system will reinforce that system in order to maintain and strengthen itself, and the ideological dimension of that strengthening generally falls to education.Further, the territory known as the Okinawa region (Ryūkyū-Okinawa) is made up of islands widely dispersed across the ocean; these islands maintain different cultures and an academically uniform grasp of this area is often difficult to achieve. It is not simply a matter of whether the law can be appropriately applied there; in actuality, these differently scaled island societies also have subtle differences among them. This article would like to limit its argument to several main points about the comparatively narrow Okinawa main island on which the Ryūkyū court existed.As this article’s title indicates, this research is concerned with actions that moved the Okinawa region (Ryūkyū-Okinawa) into modern Japanese national consciousness. It does not, however, focus on the modalities of those actions, analyzing instead how the state and central government who were under pressure to act became aware of the Okinawa region. […] In this essay, the military historical perspective refers not simply to military history as it is commonly understood. Rather, I mean it in the broader sense of the geopolitics that accompanied Okinawa’s position as a military buffer on Japan’s periphery; it includes matters like the national consciousness of the region’s inhabitants and their militarization as a matter of government policy. Put differently, this essay considers the impact of military matters on a region’s inhabitants and thereby explores the roles of the military and education in the formation of the nation-state.The Ryūkyū shobun was the event that started the political process of the Okinawa region’s annexation (heigō) into modern Japan. The Meiji state’s “Ryūkyū problem” was different from the challenges it faced in its other domestic situations. The processes of hanseki hōkan (return of registers) and haihan chiken (abolition of han and establishment of prefectures) that were key to the centralization of national authority were not implemented in Okinawa. That work was left undone and remained so for a long time but was executed in one fell swoop in the form of the Ryūkyū shobun in 1879, the historically significant beginning of the Japanese government’s creation of a shared foundation for domestic unification.1While the annexation of the Okinawa region greatly shaped both modern Japan’s subsequent trajectory and Okinawa’s unification, domestication, naichi-fication, and imperial subjectification, it was also an actual historical and political process and one that did not necessarily advance according to the government’s intentions or design. For one thing, the region thickly retained many elements and characteristics of the Ryūkyū Kingdom. The Kingdom’s old ruling class also attempted a spirited resistance against the Meiji government because they risked losing their status under the new regime. That friction went in a particular direction, but how that discord played out was the process through which the government’s policies penetrated Okinawa. Looking at the political process over a longer span of a century, we must acknowledge that the government achieved a considerable number of its aims.Yamagata Aritomo is central to this analysis because he was very much connected to modern Japan’s government and military and left a deep legacy. Yamagata left behind very important and interesting statements after visiting the Okinawa region, trips that were also military inspections. For the purpose of a concrete explanation, here is a somewhat long excerpt from Yamagata’s writing. These statements have a prophetic dimension as the Okinawa region’s subsequent development seemed to progress along the course laid out in them.2 At the same time, the text also plainly demonstrates how Okinawa was reflected in the eyes of policymakers and this is worth noting because Yamagata’s personal consciousness from his experience with Okinawa was drawn up, elevated, and expanded to the level of government policy.I (Aritomo) was this time ordered to take an inspection tour of the Okinawa islands, Gotō, and Tsushima and the like. In the actual situation of the islands that I observed, new initiatives or additional improvements are necessary for their administration. Places like the Okinawa islands and Amami Ōshima are blessed even with natural good harbors but simply have very few products. It is probably necessary to make trade prosper in the future. As in the case of two of Okinawa’s outlying islands of Miyako and Yaeyama, only awa millet, cloth, soot, and coal are produced. The Gotō islands and Tsushima also possess many harbors. In particular, Tsushima is a strategic place very close to Korea. The state must therefore give these islands adequate protection and cultivate their resources. On top of that defenses must be rigorously prepared. Looking at the international situation that surrounds Japan, the East, namely East Asia presents the tensest circumstances. Relations between Qing China and Korea3 are already strained, the Sino-French war has broken out, and British-Russo frictions are also seething. title: The Lincoln-McClellan Relationship in Myth and Memory
venue: The Journal of the Abraham Lincoln Association
abstract: Like many Civil War historians, I have for many years accepted invitations to address the general public. I have nearly always tried to offer fresh perspectives, and these have generally been well received. But almost invariably the Q and A or personal exchanges reveal an affection for familiar stories or questions. (Prominent among them is the query “What if Stonewall Jackson had been present at Gettysburg?”)For a long time I harbored a private condescension about this affection, coupled with complete incuriosity about what its significance might be. But eventually I came to believe that I was missing something important: that these familiar stories, endlessly retold in nearly the same ways, were expressions of a mythic view of the Civil War, what the amateur historian Otto Eisenschiml memorably labeled “the American Iliad.”1For Eisenschiml “the American Iliad” was merely a clever title for a compendium of eyewitness accounts of the conflict, but I take the term seriously. In Homer’s Iliad the anger of Achilles, the perfidy of Agamemnon, the doomed gallantry of Hector—and the relationships between them—have enormous, uncontested, unchanging, and almost primal symbolic meaning. So too do certain figures in the American Iliad. Prominent among these are the butcher Grant, the Christ-like Lee, and the rage-filled Sherman. I believe that the traditional Civil War narrative functions as a national myth of central importance to our understanding of ourselves as Americans. And like the classic mythologies of old, it contains timeless wisdom about what it means to be a human being. Homer’s Iliad tells us much about war but also much about life. The American Iliad does the same thing.For me the most compelling clue to this mythic American Iliad was my puzzlement over the unusually rigid portrayal of the vexed command partnership between Abraham Lincoln and George B. McClellan. It’s one of the Civil War’s most familiar episodes, perhaps far too familiar. Indeed, for at least seven decades, the basic outline of the story has remained unchanged. That’s unusual for an important historical subject, especially since we historians are often accused of ceaseless revisionism.The two principals are men with starkly contrasting reputations. In popular imagination, Lincoln is the man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, who through patience and perseverance leads the country through the four bloodiest years of its existence. He breaks the chains of four million enslaved Americans. He nobly saves the Union, the last, best hope of earth. And in the hour of final victory he perishes a martyr, his memory forever enshrined in the heart of every patriotic American.McClellan’s image is almost the polar opposite. If Lincoln is a secular saint, McClellan is the arrogant narcissist, the hubristic “Young Napoleon.” He dreams of saving the republic, yet proves so timid in battle, so self-pitying in defeat, and above all so disdainful of Lincoln that he is widely despised—and held completely to blame for the ultimate failure of the relationship between Lincoln and himself. When historian Thomas J. Rowland told friends that he had embarked on a new study of McClellan, even those only casually acquainted with the Civil War knew enough to loathe “Little Mac.” “At the very mention of McClellan’s name,” he wrote, “a visage of contempt generally crept over their other otherwise benevolent gazes, or worse, they mimed sticking their fingers down their throats.”2The rigid portrayal has seeped into popular culture as well. Journalists routinely invoke it when appraising the relationships between modern commanders in chief and key subordinates, invariably extolling the former and excoriating the latter. During the Afghanistan and Iraq wars, analogies to Lincoln and McClellan appeared in the media at least ninety times.3 Retired lieutenant general Ricardo Sanchez, who had led U.S. forces in Iraq in 2003–4, was labeled “Bush’s McClellan” for his criticisms of the George W. Bush administration’s handling of the war in 2007. Invoking a common comparison, the timidity of McClellan contrasted with the killer instinct of Ulysses S. Grant, one op-ed writer queried acidly, “Is this the sour grapes of a failed McClellan shown up by a U. S. Grant?” “McClellan,” the writer continued, “was famously fired by President Lincoln after being repeatedly outwitted by Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee in the Civil War. Once Gen. Ulysses S. Grant was placed in charge, things soon turned around—kind of like Iraq today under Gen. David Petraeus.”4When General Stanley McChrystal replaced General David McKiernan as commander of U.S. forces in Afghanistan in June 2009, Investor’s Business Daily compared McKiernan’s relief favorably to Grant’s replacement of McClellan. “Changing commanders in the middle of a war is sometimes a necessary prelude to victory,” noted the editorial. “Union fortunes were bleak in the summer of 1864 until President Abraham Lincoln sacked the pedestrian Gen. George McClellan and chose Gen. Ulysses S. Grant to command Union forces and pointed Gen. William T. Sherman toward Atlanta.”5 To be sure, this was garbled history. McClellan was relieved of command in November 1862; Grant did not become general-in-chief until March 1864 (and the general had “pointed Sherman toward Atlanta” months before the summer of that year). It is also more likely that Lincoln sacked McClellan for political rather than military reasons. But the key charge against McClellan—that he was unforgivably overcautious—is the salient feature of the usual portrayal of the Lincoln-McClellan relationship. If Lincoln comes in for editorial criticism (which happens infrequently), it is for too long sticking with McClellan “after there was abundant evidence that his general lacked the aggressive spirit needed to win the war.”6Ironically, a year later McChrystal abruptly went from being a contemporary Grant to being a contemporary McClellan. When President Barack Obama forced McChrystal into retirement after the latter accused senior administration officials of hobbling his ability to win the conflict, some commentators compared the president’s action to Lincoln’s relief of McClellan. It was “not the first time in our nation’s history that presidents and generals have clashed,” the Oakland Tribune reminded readers. “In 1862, it was Abraham Lincoln who fired Gen. Nearly a century later, faced with General Douglas MacArthur’s repeated public criticisms of President Harry S Truman’s decision to keep the Korean War carefully limited—MacArthur famously having declared, “There is no substitute for victory,” and hinting broadly that the United States should employ nuclear weapons to resolve the conflict—Truman relieved MacArthur in April 1951. In his memoirs, Truman likened his decision to Lincoln’s sacking of McClellan after the general’s chronic refusal to assume the offensive. Truman claimed he sent a staff member to the Library of Congress to study Lincoln’s troubles with McClellan and write a report. “Lincoln was patient,” Truman wrote, “for that was his nature, but at long last he was compelled to relieve the Union Army’s principal commander.
